claude.sample_unit: open-ended HSCT questions submitted to each LLM

links.outcome: Accuracy and verifiability of sources and citations supplied by LLMs
links.effect: ChatGPT-3.5 gave no verifiable sources; ChatGPT-4 referenced literature in 10/21 (48%) evaluable cases, frequently out-of-date or with inaccurate authorship, title, or DOI; broken URLs reported.
links.quote: ChatGPT-4 referenced scientific literature in 10 of 21 (48%) evaluable cases, frequently with relevant but out-of-date papers, or with inaccurate authorship, title, or Digital Object Identifier.

links.outcome: Hallucinated clinical content in ungrounded LLM answers
links.effect: All models hallucinated: at least 1 hallucinated answer in 7/24 (29%) ChatGPT-3.5, 3/7 (43%) ChatGPT-4, and 14/27 (52%) Bard evaluable cases.
links.quote: All exhibited episodes of hallucinations, with ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4, and Bard showing at least 1 hallucinated answer in 7 of 24 (29%), 3 of 7 (43%), and 14 of 27 (52%) of evaluable cases, respectively.

links.outcome: Language appropriateness of patient-targeted LLM answers
links.effect: ChatGPT-4 used excessively technical language, only 10/22 (46%) rated appropriate vs 17/21 (81%) for ChatGPT-3.5 (P=.03).
links.quote: however, ChatGPT-4 showed excessively technical language, with only 10 of 22 (46%) rated as “3” in language appropriateness compared to 17 of 21 (81%) for ChatGPT-3.5.

links.outcome: Veracity of LLM answers against reference handbooks
links.effect: Veracity rated correct in 58/66 (88%) ChatGPT-4, 40/54 (74%) ChatGPT-3.5, 16/63 (25%) Bard (P<.001).
links.quote: ChatGPT-4 performed best in terms of veracity, with 58 of 66 (88%) of answers considered correct (rated as “3”), followed by ChatGPT-3.5 (40/54, 74%) and Bard (16/63, 25%; P <.001).

links.outcome: Reproducibility of responses across repeated submissions
links.effect: Consistent responses in 66/72 (92%) ChatGPT-4, 54/72 (75%) ChatGPT-3.5, 63/69 (91%) Bard (P=.007).
links.quote: ChatGPT-4 had the highest rate of consistent responses (66/72, 92%) followed by Bard (63/69, 91%) and ChatGPT-3.5 (54/72, 75%; P =.007).

links.outcome: LLM calculation of established risk scores
links.effect: LLMs were ineffective at calculating well-established risk scores such as the HCT-specific Comorbidity Index.
links.quote: The LLMs also proved ineffective at calculating well-established risk scores (eg, Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation–specific Comorbidity Index).

links.effect: Consistent responses: ChatGPT-4 66/72 (92%), Bard 63/69 (91%), ChatGPT-3.5 54/72 (75%; P=.007).
links.quote: ChatGPT-4 had the highest rate of consistent responses (66/72, 92%) followed by Bard (63/69, 91%) and ChatGPT-3.5 (54/72, 75%; P =.007).

links.effect: Correct veracity ratings: ChatGPT-4 58/66 (88%), ChatGPT-3.5 40/54 (74%), Bard 16/63 (25%; P<.001).
links.quote: ChatGPT-4 performed best in terms of veracity, with 58 of 66 (88%) of answers considered correct (rated as “3”), followed by ChatGPT-3.5 (40/54, 74%) and Bard (16/63, 25%; P <.001).

links.effect: At least 1 hallucinated answer occurred in ChatGPT-3.5 7/24 (29%), ChatGPT-4 3/7 (43%), Bard 14/27 (52%).
links.quote: All exhibited episodes of hallucinations, with ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4, and Bard showing at least 1 hallucinated answer in 7 of 24 (29%), 3 of 7 (43%), and 14 of 27 (52%) of evaluable cases, respectively.

links.effect: ChatGPT-3.5 gave no verifiable sources; ChatGPT-4 cited literature in 10/21 (48%) cases, often out-of-date or inaccurate.
links.quote: ChatGPT-3.5 did not provide verifiable information sources despite the prompt requiring them to do so, reporting “The information I provide is based on the knowledge I was trained on until September 2021”; ChatGPT-4 referenced scientific literature in 10 of 21 (48%) evaluable cases, frequently with relevant but out-of-date papers, or with inaccurate authorship, title, or Digital Object Identifier.

links.effect: ChatGPT-4 language appropriateness was 10/22 (46%) rated “3” versus ChatGPT-3.5 17/21 (81%).
links.quote: however, ChatGPT-4 showed excessively technical language, with only 10 of 22 (46%) rated as “3” in language appropriateness compared to 17 of 21 (81%) for ChatGPT-3.5.

links.effect: Consistent responses occurred in 92% (66/72) for ChatGPT-4, 91% (63/69) for Bard, and 75% (54/72) for ChatGPT-3.5 (P=.007).
links.quote: ChatGPT-4 had the highest rate of consistent responses (66/72, 92%) followed by Bard (63/69, 91%) and ChatGPT-3.5 (54/72, 75%; P =.007).

links.outcome: Accuracy and verifiability of scientific citations
links.effect: ChatGPT-4 cited scientific literature in 48% (10/21) of evaluable cases, frequently with inaccurate authorship, title, DOI, or out-of-date papers.
links.quote: ChatGPT-3.5 did not provide verifiable information sources despite the prompt requiring them to do so, reporting “The information I provide is based on the knowledge I was trained on until September 2021”; ChatGPT-4 referenced scientific literature in 10 of 21 (48%) evaluable cases, frequently with relevant but out-of-date papers, or with inaccurate authorship, title, or Digital Object Identifier.

screen.practice: audience-adapted prompting with source citation request
screen.reason: The study tests LLM performance on HSCT questions and explicitly evaluates prompting interventions to adapt language to specific target audiences (clinicians vs patients) and require verifiable sources of information.

primary.practice: audience-tailored prompting and source attribution prompting
